claims.text: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy has a fine lamellar microstructure containing coupled FCC and B2 phases.
The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibits high strength and ductility at room temperature.
FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition during intermediate-to-high-temperature aging.
Evolution of local chemical order and phase-boundary morphology drives the transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
Intermediate aging forms or preserves coherent ordered B2 domains with enhanced chemical short-range order.
Chemical short-range order reduces the mobility of screw dislocations.
Chemical short-range order impedes dislocation cross-slip.
Enhanced chemical short-range order promotes cross-slip locking of screw dislocations.
Cross-slip locking occurs during screw-dislocation motion and can provide additional strengthening in refractory high-entropy alloys.
SRO-induced cross-slip locking and reduced dislocation mobility cause embrittlement at intermediate aging temperatures.
Higher-temperature aging causes B2 domains to coarsen or lose coherence.
Increasing temperature attenuates the resistance to screw-dislocation motion associated with short-range order.
B2 coarsening or loss of coherence restores dislocation mobility and ductility at higher aging temperatures.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism operates within grain interiors through dislocation-order interactions rather than through impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
The embrittlement regime is approximately associated with intermediate aging temperatures of 400-600 degrees Celsius.
The lower and upper boundaries of the embrittlement regime correspond respectively to maximized B2 ordering while domains remain coherent and to the onset of B2 coarsening or coherence loss.
The ductile-brittle-ductile transition occurs without significant grain coarsening or grain-boundary impurity segregation.
If grain-boundary embrittlement is dominant, the loss of ductility should correlate with impurity segregation at grain boundaries rather than with evolution of local chemical order.
